data.title: Maroš Demko: The Kyiv Pantheon – the Slavic gods of Prince Vladimir
data.excerpt: Published with the author's permission: a study of the Slavic gods by Mgr. Maroš Demko, which first appeared in the journal MEDEA II in 1998. It asks why Prince Vladimir set up idols of Perun, Chors, Dažbog, Stribog, Simargl and Mokoš in Kyiv in 980, what the functions of these gods were and why others are missing from his list.
data.metaTitle: The Kyiv Pantheon: Vladimir's Slavic Gods
data.metaDescription: A study by Maroš Demko on the Kyiv pantheon of Slavic gods, the six idols Prince Vladimir set up in 980. First published in MEDEA II in 1998.

timeline.title: The reign of Prince Svyatoslav
timeline.description: The Rus land was divided among his three sons: Yaropolk in Kyiv, Oleg in the land of the Drevlians and Vladimir in Novgorod.

timeline.title: Yaropolk defeats Oleg
timeline.description: Yaropolk marched against Oleg and killed him in battle; Vladimir feared for his own person and fled overseas to the Varangians.

timeline.title: Vladimir establishes the Kyiv pantheon
timeline.description: Vladimir defeated and killed Yaropolk, began to rule in Kyiv alone and on a hill by the princely court set up idols of Perun, Chors, Dažbog, Stribog, Simargl and Mokoš.

timeline.title: Human sacrifices
timeline.description: Povesť vremennych let records a report of human sacrifices for this year.

timeline.title: The acceptance of Christianity
timeline.description: Vladimir accepted Christianity, probably after the failure of the state pagan cult; the idols were destroyed and the statue of Veles was thrown into the river Pochaina.

timeline.title: Excavation of the sacrificial site at Peryň
timeline.description: The excavation led by V. V. Sedov uncovered, at a place called Peryň near Novgorod, a circular ditch with eight niches for fire and a pit left by an idol – evidence of a cult place of Perun.

children.text: With the author's permission we bring you this fine article on the Slavic gods, written by Mgr. Maroš Demko. The article appeared in the journal MEDEA II in 1998. The images were added later by me and were not part of the original article. Orgoň
Maroš Demko : THE KYIV PANTHEON

At the outset of this study I consider it necessary to set out a few historical facts about Kyivan Rus. Already in the lifetime of Prince Svyatoslav (941–973) the Rus land was divided among his three sons. After Svyatoslav's death (973) there remained - Yaropolk in Kyiv, Oleg in the land of the Drevlians and Vladimir in Novgorod. In 977 Yaropolk marched against Oleg and Oleg was killed in the battle. Vladimir, who feared for his own person, fled overseas, where he hired a military detachment of Varangians. In 980 Vladimir set out from Novgorod with the Varangians and defeated and killed Yaropolk. 1
The following report from Povesť vremennych let (the Primary Chronicle) is also linked to the year 980: “
I nača kňažiti Volodimer v Kijeve jedin, i postavi kumiry na cholmu vne dvora teremnago: Peruna dreviana, a glavu jego srebrenu a us zlat, i Chrsa, Dažboga i Striboga i Simargla i Mokoš

This report is one of the most frequently cited pieces of evidence for the existence of the old Slavic gods in Kyivan Rus. It caught my attention because of the several questions attached to it: Why did Vladimir set up idols of pagan gods on a hill in the middle of Kyiv? Why precisely these gods? What were their functions? Why are other gods missing here? I shall attempt to answer these questions in my study, my basic premise being that I take the chronicle entry to be a truthful picture of reality.

Forming a picture of the Slavic gods and of Slavic religion is not easy. The main reason for the difficulty is the lack of sufficient information. The sources for our knowledge of the Slavic gods can be divided into three groups:
 
 1. Written sources and linguistic analysis.
 2. Archaeological finds.
 3. Ethnographic records. 
 
 The main source of knowledge of Slavic religion is the written sources. These are reports recorded for the most part by Christian monks and missionaries, or by Arab travellers and Byzantine writers, which considerably limits their value as testimony. No stories about the origin of the world, of the gods and of people, or of other mythical beings have survived, as they have among other peoples of Europe. The possibilities for scholarly study of Slavic religion are comparable with the situation that prevails in the study of the religion of the Balts or of the continental Celts.

children.text:
The oldest report on the religious ideas of the Slavs is given by the Byzantine historian Procopius of Caesarea in his book The Gothic War in the 6th century AD. He writes of the Slavs' veneration of a single god - the ruler of lightning - to whom they bring offerings, including cattle.3 From the 10th century (the year 922) comes the report of the Arab traveller Ibn Fadlan, who describes the funeral of a Rus magnate. Concrete ideas about the afterlife among the Slavs, and data on offerings and temples on heights, were left to us by al-Masudi. 4 
 
 A great many reports are provided by Russian sources of the 11th and 12th centuries. An important source is the chronicle Povesť vremenných let already mentioned. Further mentions appear in numerous tracts that arose as instructions for the clergy in the struggle against pagan customs and ideas - Slovo i otkrovenije sv. apostol, Reč filozofa k Vladimírovi Veľkému (The Philosopher's Speech to Vladimir the Great), Slovo sv. Grigorija Bogoslova, Choždenije Bogorodici and others.5 An important position is held by Slovo o pluku Igorovom (The Tale of Igor's Campaign) - a heroic epic from the end of the 12th century, in which some details appear that supplement the data of the chronicles. 
 
 Extensive, too, are the sources informing us about the religion of the West Slavic tribes. The oldest of them is the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg, from the years 1012–1018, which gives data on the tribe of the Lutici-Redarians and their sanctuary at Rethra. Adam of Bremen also writes about Rethra and other places in the years 1074–1076. Further sources from the 12th century are the three biographies of Bishop Otto of Bamberg, written by Ebo, Herbord and an anonymous monk of the monastery at Prüfening, and finally the Chronicle of the Slavs (Chronica Slavorum) by Helmold, the priest of Bosau. A great deal of data was recorded in his Deeds of the Danes (Gesta Danorum) by the priest of Saxon origin Saxo Grammaticus, and certain insights about the gods of the Baltic Slavs are brought by a source of Nordic origin as well - the Knýtlinga saga. 6

Fragments of myths preserved in oral tradition, and folk beliefs and customs marked by Christianity, are known to us from numerous ethnographic records of the 18th to 20th centuries. The third kind of source - archaeological finds - supplements the preceding data. Archaeological finds, whose stock is far from being as exhausted as the ethnographic and linguistic records, represent the future of new data on the Slavic gods and religion. From the mosaic assembled from these three kinds of sources there arises a picture of Slavic religion, of the gods and of their functions. Evidence for the spread of the cult of individual gods is provided by geographical names derived from the names of these gods.
Perun

The first god listed in Vladimir's inventory is Perun. He alone also has a description of his idol attached - wooden, with a silver head and golden moustache. At the same time as the idols were set up in Kyiv, Vladimir sent his uncle Dobrynya to Novgorod: “And Dobrynya came to Novgorod, set up an idol above the river Volkhov, and the people of Novgorod made offerings to him.”7 The privileged position of Perun - as the head of the Kyiv pantheon - is confirmed by further written reports as well, in which he is mentioned far more often than other gods. The first mention that could relate to Perun comes from the pen of the above-mentioned Procopius in the 6th century. Even though Procopius does not give a name, he most probably meant Perun, although we cannot rule out the name of another god either - Rod, for example.8 In the Byzantine legend the Life of St Demetrius of Thessaloniki, from the 7th century AD, the name Perun appears for the first time, which supports the hypothesis that Procopius's report concerns the same god as well.9 Important reports, however, come directly from Kyivan Rus, where Povesť vremennych let gives Perun as the guarantor of the Byzantine–Rus treaties of 907, 912, 946 and 971: “ ... i muži jego po Ruskomu zakonu kľašasja oružjem svojim, i Perunom, bogom svojim i Volosom, skotjem bogom”.10

Perun's name also occurs very often in the later anti-pagan instructional texts of Russian Christian literature. He is mentioned among the West Slavs as well - in Helmold's chronicle, and Saxo Grammaticus likewise gives Perun's son - Porenutius.11

Perun represents the figure of the thunder god widespread among all the Indo-European peoples (Zeus, Taranis, Thor and others). His name is derived from the Indo-European root per(k/g), which means to strike, to hit, to beat, to lash.12 The linguistic kinship with the Latvian Perkons, the Lithuanian Perkunas and further linguistic correspondences (Gr. - keraunos, peraunos; Ind. - Parjanya; Celt. - hercynia and others) point to the antiquity of this god. The beginnings of his cult are sought as early as the period of Balto-Slavic unity.

Perun's sacred tree was the oak, as Constantine Porphyrogenitus also informs us.13 The oak was venerated as a sacred tree among most Indo-European peoples, chiefly in connection with the thunder god. From toponymy it is possible to assume places of veneration of Perun on hills, and whole oak groves were probably dedicated to him (Perunova dubrava in Dalmatia, Perunova gora in Poland, Perun gora in Serbia, etc.).14 As is known from the sources too, animals were sacrificed to Perun - cattle, cockerels, hens and horses, whose skeletons have also been found in archaeological excavations.15 Human sacrifices are known as well, spoken of by a report in Povesť vremennych let for the year 983.16 Bloodless offerings included gifts of grain, bread, cheese and honey, or libations of milk and wine, which are documented in ethnographic records right down to the 19th century.17

Evidence of a cult place - a sacrificial site - was brought by the archaeological excavations of 1951–52 led by V. V. Sedov. In the north of the former Kyivan Rus, close to Novgorod, at a place called Peryň, a circular ditch was found with eight niches in which fire used to burn, and in whose centre there was a pit left by an idol.18 Perun's attributes included the axe, especially the “fiery axe”, which was called strela (‘arrow’). Amulets in the form of an axe are a frequent archaeological find of the 10th to 14th centuries.19 The axe and its connection with fertility played an important role in the folk beliefs of the Slavic and Baltic peoples right down to the 20th century, as a great many ethnographic records attest.20 After the acceptance of Christianity the veneration of Perun passed to St Elijah, depicted as a white-bearded old man travelling across the sky in a fiery chariot.21 The transposition of the myth into a heroic tale can be observed in the Russian byliny about Ilya Muromets, who became the bearer of Perun's attributes.22

Although further evidence of the veneration of Perun is known, I think the evidence given above is sufficient to determine the functions of this god in Slavic religion. The original function of the thunder god spread, by way of the god of the fertilising storm, as far as the god of fertility and of the harvest. In the time of Kyivan Rus - the period of Vladimir - the function of the god of warriors came to the fore, and by Vladimir himself he was raised to the highest god in the state cult. The aspect of guarantor of treaties, of the Mithra or Old Germanic Tyr type, is interesting as well.
Dažbog

In the written sources we first encounter Dažbog (Dazhbog) in Povesť vremennych let precisely in connection with the Kyiv pantheon. In the Russian translation of the Chronicle of John Malalas, Dažbog is designated as the son of Svarog and identified with the sun.23 The importance of this god is also attested by his occurrence in Slovo o pluku Igorovom, where the Rus are called Dažbog's grandsons. Further Russian tracts of the 11th to 12th centuries, for example Slovo sv. Jána Zlatoústeho (the Homily of St John Chrysostom), speak of veneration of fire called Svarožic (Svarozhits).24 In the chronicle of Thietmar of Merseburg a wooden sanctuary, Riedigost, among the tribe of the Redarians is described. Inside stood a statue of Svarožic in military armour.25

The name Dažbog consists of two components - daž and bog. Besides the meaning ‘god’, the word bog may also have the secondary meaning of share, portion, rich, related to the Russian bogat, ubog or the Vedic bhaga.26 Daž is an imperative from dať, to give.27 A connection with the Indo-European root dag (Old Indian dah) = to burn cannot be ruled out either.28 Svarožic is a name derived from the patronymic Svarog and means Svarog's son.29

Statues of Dažbog, or rather of Svarožic, were mentioned in Kyiv and in Rethra-Riedigost. Among the tribe of the Redarians Svarožic became the highest tribal god, who had his central temple at Rethra. In connection with fire, an interesting mention of the Slavs has survived from the pen of the Arab traveller Gardizi: “They are all worshippers of fire, they grow chiefly millet, and at the harvest they take the millet out of the vessels onto spoons, raise [them] to heaven [with the words] ‘o lord, thou who hast given us food, give us abundance now also.‘ ”30 The relationship between fire and fertility would correspond to the function of Dažbog as the god of the good, kindly sun, the giver of life.

Ethnography attests a generally widespread cult of fire among all the Slavic peoples. Among the special Christmas customs preserved among the South Slavs was the burning of the trunk or of a branch of a tree, called badnik or mlaď bog among the Bulgarians and božič among the Slovenes.31 The burning of St John's fires is known in the territory of present-day Slovakia as well. The prelude to these festivities was the night of St Philip and St James, likewise connected with the burning of fires, which was to protect the harvest and the cattle from the spells of witches.32 In the Balkans they knew Dabog or Dajbog, the giver of all good.33 As the cult animal of Dažbog-Svarožic we can certainly identify the white horse (Svarožic's sacred oracular horse at Rethra)34, which among all the Indo-Europeans is regarded as a solar symbol. In Russian folklore the image of Jarilo (the spring aspect of the sun god) has survived, riding on a white horse, dressed in a white cloak with a crown of meadow flowers.35
Dažbog probably represented a solar deity of the Apollo type and also encompassed the function of the giver god (deus dator).
Chors

The name Chors (Khors) appears in the sources also in the forms Chros, Chrs, Chres or Churs.36 Besides Povesť vremennych let, he is mentioned by the apocrypha Choždenije bogorodici, Slovo i otkrovenije sv. apostol, Beseda trech svjatiteľej and others.37 An important mention occurs in Slovo o pluku Igorovom, where it is said of Prince Vseslav that he ran by night like a wolf from Kyiv to Tmutarakan and before dawn crossed the path of “great Chors”.38

Most scholars assume that Chors is of Iranian origin and connect him with the Persian xor, xores, xoršid, which means shining sun.39 Some researchers, for example A. Brückner, derive his name from the Proto-Slavic krš = gaunt, and point to his connection with the moon.40

Apart from the single mention in Povesť vremennych let relating precisely to the Kyiv pantheon, there are no further data on any special cult of this god. We learn of the great significance of the sun among the Slavs from ethnographic records. Solar symbols adorning Russian houses, and the so-called krasnyj ugol - a special sacred space inside the house connected with the sun - testify to the great significance of the sun in Russian folklore.41

The construct of some researchers pointing to a connection of Chors with the moon is contradicted by the slight significance attached to the moon among the Indo-European peoples, and likewise by the fact that some Old Russian legends describe the moon as a beautiful young woman whom the sun marries at the beginning of summer, abandons in winter and returns to in spring.
I incline to the view that Chors represented a solar deity (a sun god), comparable with the Greek Helios.
Stribog

Apart from the mention in Povesť vremennych let for the year 980, Stribog occurs in the written sources only twice. In the Russian translation of the Homily of St John Chrysostom he is mentioned alongside Dažbog and Pereplut.42 The second mention is found in Slovo o pluku Igorovom, where the winds are called Stribog's grandsons.

The etymology of his name is unclear and the opinions of researchers are varied. Some researchers derive it from the Iranian Sríbagha = beautiful god, which was an epithet of the Old Persian Ahura Mazda.43 A different view is held, for example, by V. N. Toporov, who derives it from ptribhagos and this in turn from the more original pater dieus, with ptri changing to stri and dieus to bhagos. A further group of researchers derives it from the Proto-Slavic streti, i.e. to grow numb (under the influence of an icy wind).44 Another explanation is offered by Berneker - from stroj, striti, which would indicate the function of a steward of goods.45

Apart from the mention of the idol in Kyiv, no other reports of the cult of this god are known. From the few data we have, we can speak of his functions only on a hypothetical level. Since his idol was set up in Kyiv alongside other gods, we may assume that he is one of the higher gods. The mention in Slovo o pluku Igorovom suggests his connection with the atmosphere. Of the etymological theories, Berneker's seems the most probable, that is, the function of a steward of goods. The occurrence of the name Stribog together with Dažbog in the Homily of St John Chrysostom might point to this as well.46
Simargl
In the Russian sources the name of this god is attested as Simargl, Semargl, Sejmarekľ, but Slovo nekojego christoljubca gives, alongside Perun and Mokoš, two gods, Sim and Rgl.47

The etymological explanations therefore divide into two directions. The first, based on a single-word name, derives his origin from the Iranian senmurv-símurg.48 On the evidence of Slovo nekojego christoľjubca, A. Bruckner interprets Sim and Rgl as two deities, probably divine twins, and derives their names from the Slavic words sem-semja = family, or siemenje = seed, and Rgla from the Proto-Slavic rež = rye, or the Lithuanian rugti, Polish rug = leaven, to ferment.49 He supports his hypothesis with the occurrence of Polish and Lithuanian local geographical names derived from the names of these gods.50 Other explanations of the name Simargl are known too. V. Ivanov and V. Toporov see in it a seven-headed deity, “semiglav”.51 Even more speculative are the hypotheses that it is a corruption of the goddesses Asimat and Ergel (or Nergal) from Mesopotamia, or of the Graeco-Egyptian Sem-Heracles.52

Again, apart from the idol that stood in Kyiv, we know of no verified reports or finds speaking of the cult of this god. The theory of a cult of divine twins may be confirmed by the find of a wooden idol from Fischerinsel in the Tollensee near Neubrandenburg.53 However, the great distance between the find spot and the written record weakens this theory. On the contrary, the occurrence of depictions of the mythological motif of a winged dog on silver bracelets, kolts and diadems of the 11th–13th centuries from the eastern Dnieper region supports the Iranian origin of Simargl.54 Similar depictions are known from the late Sasanian period (7th–8th centuries AD) in Iran.55

The Iranian Saena-simurgh is known from Mazdaist texts as an enormous bird that sits on the top of the tree of all seeds and by beating its wings scatters the seed.56 In Firdausi's Book of Kings the king of birds Simurgh appears, who is the protector of the hero Rustam.57 From the mythological significance of Simurgh in Iran his functions in Slavic religion are also derived. Rybakov regards him as the protector of plants and roots and the companion of the goddess Mokoš.58 M. Gimbutas derives his name from the Sarmatian supreme god Simarg and connects him with the function of a warrior god whose veneration passed in Slavic folklore to the eagle.59 The pair Sim and Rgl is regarded by V. Pisani as the protectors of cattle (Sim) and of grain (Rgl).60
Mokoš

The last deity closing the Kyiv pantheon was Mokoš (Mokosh). She is thus the only female goddess included in Vladimir's list of gods. Her name is known from numerous Russian sources as well, for example Slovo sv. Jána Zlatoústeho, Slovo nekojego christoljubca, Slovo sv. Grigorija and others.61

There are several views on the etymology of her name. A Finnish origin from the name Mokša, Mokš, Moks among the Mordvin tribe, as Anichkov suggests, seems improbable.62 Equally hard to accept is the connection with the Indian makha (exalted) or mokša (salvation).63 The most probable is the derivation of her name from the Slavic root mok, mokr = wet, damp.64 Rybakov gives the etymology of the name Mokoš from koš, kš, which means lot, blow, fate.65

We learn of the great significance of the cult of Mokoš as late as the 16th century, when a priest asked women at confession whether they had gone to Mokoš.66 The memory of Mokoš was preserved in folk tradition in Ukraine and the north of Russia right down to the 19th century.67 People imagined her as a woman with a large head and long arms who spins at night.68 After the acceptance of Christianity the veneration of Mokoš passed to Paraskeva-Pyatnitsa, which suggests that Friday was the day dedicated to the goddess and connected with ritual prohibitions of women's work on that day.69 From the regions of Pskov, Novgorod and Chernihiv local names such as Makuši, Makušina, Makušovo are known, attesting to the spread of her cult.70 The hill Mokošín in Bohemia is also known.71

Mokoš was probably the personification of the damp, fertile earth, rooted in Russian culture under the name mať syraja zemlja. An analogy to this Slavic goddess can be found in the Iranian goddess Anahita, whose epithet Aredvi meant damp.
A very interesting fact is that the god
Veles

- Volos was missing from the Kyiv pantheon. He too belonged among the important Old Russian gods, as can be seen from the above-mentioned report about the oaths of the Rus at the conclusion of the Byzantine-Rus treaties. His name appears in two records - for the years 907 and 971, always with the epithet skotij bog, i.e. the god of cattle. It is possible that, as the god of the oath of the Varangian princes, he is of Scandinavian origin and is etymologically related to Volsi (the sacred horse phallus used in Nordic magic to secure fertility).72 Traces of his cult, however, can also be found among the other Slavic peoples in local names and in folk sayings and songs.73 His connection with the Lithuanian Velinas, Vels - terms connected with death (vele = the shade of death, velines = the days of death) - is therefore more probable.74

In folk religion a god of death can often acquire chthonic connotations with wealth, and so encompass the functions of a giver and protector in wealth as well. In the Christian era Veles was identified with St Vlasij (Blaise), precisely thanks to the Byzantine veneration of St Blaise as the protector of flocks.75

In Slovo o pluku Igorovom the singer Boyan is designated as Veles's grandson. This reveals to us a deeper prophetic nature of Veles, and Veles thus takes on certain features identical with those of Odin.76 In this way we could admit certain Scandinavian influences on Slavic religion, and perhaps it was precisely through this influence that the form Volos spread instead of the more original Veles.77

Much more evidence of the veneration of Veles could be given (figurines of phallic shape, numerous ethnographic records), but that is not my aim. The data given are sufficient to determine the functions of Veles in Old Russian religion. Veles represented an old Slavic god of death or of the underworld. Through the development of folk belief he acquired the features of a giver and protector of wealth, and in the Varangian substratum he could become an interpretation of Odin.

Other important Old Russian deities (Rod and the rožanice, Svarog) are missing from the Kyiv pantheon as well. Explaining their absence and attempting to answer the questions posed in the introduction will form the conclusion of my study.
Conclusion

Above all it must be borne in mind that the content of the religious ideas and customs of any religion is in constant development, and that a report relating to a particular period captures only the momentary state of the religion in question. It is therefore necessary to direct attention to the historical circumstances relating to the period of Vladimir's rule in Kyivan Rus and to the historical situation itself in this period. Kyivan Rus at that time already represented a developed feudal state with an advanced social hierarchy.

The beginning of Vladimir's reign falls, as we can see in the introduction, in the period when the integrity of princely power was starting to disintegrate. That was probably the reason why Vladimir sought, in support of centralised power, to introduce a unified ideology in the form of a state pagan religion. Perhaps it was precisely the failure of this attempt that led Vladimir in 988 to accept Christianity. That this was an attempt to introduce a state cult is evident also from the fact that the new idols were not set up on a hill near Kyiv (as the statue of Perun under Igor), but directly in the centre of the city in the vicinity of the princely palace.78 State-wide rites and offerings were an occasion for meetings of the boyars - Vladimir's retinue - at which political questions were discussed.79 The creation of this state pantheon of gods was thus influenced by the function it was to fulfil. The chosen gods had to satisfy the religious needs of a broad spectrum of people.

Perun was suitable for the high strata of the boyars, and likewise for the Varangian detachments of warriors, who identified him with Thor. His popularity among the rest of the Slavic population too allowed Vladimir to place precisely this god in the highest position. Dažbog, Chors and most probably Stribog as well represented the uranic sphere of the pantheon, and Mokoš in turn the chthonic part. Simargl could, in connection with fertility, belong to Mokoš, or in the function of a warrior god to Perun. A merging of these two aspects is possible as well.

At the same time we can observe the relationships of the individual gods to their geographical distribution. Perun as the supreme god was suitable not only for the Varangian warriors, but also for the neighbouring Baltic tribes (Perkunas). Chors and Simargl have relationships to the southern regions because of their origin in Iran. The existence of features shared with the religion of the northern Finnic tribes is demonstrated by the goddess Mokoš. Mutual influence could have taken place from one side or the other. A greater focus on topographic research into the occurrence of the individual names would considerably help to clarify this question. All the deities are somehow connected with fertility and good, which we can interpret as meaning that they were to bring abundance and prosperity for the whole state.

As regards the non-participation of other gods in Vladimir's inventory, it is possible to explain this by the decline in the significance of some gods. Svarog, designated as Dažbog's father, probably represented in an earlier period the highest uranic deity - the creator god. His function was taken over in a later period by Dažbog, and Svarog found himself in the background, in the position of a deus otiosus.

Rod and the rožanice likewise represented an ancient deity. Rod is etymologically related to roditi, to give birth, and could represent the god who begets all things, gods and people. But through gradual development he found himself in the same position as Svarog.80 Both were pushed out of the leading position by Perun, whose function as the god of warriors became more essential in the course of historical development. Their cult was preserved only in folk belief and customs.

It is interesting that at approximately the same time the cult of Perun was not as significant among the West Slavic tribes as in Russia, and that he too probably found himself in the west in the position of a deus otiosus. We may therefore consider the influence of the Varangian warriors, venerating Thor, who in the Slavic milieu transferred his cult onto Perun, and thus his high position was preserved.

Explaining the non-participation of Veles is a more difficult problem. His occurrence in the peace treaties points to the importance of his cult in those times. In Kyiv a statue of Veles even stood in Vladimir's time, and after the acceptance of Christianity Vladimir had it thrown into the river Pochaina.81 Perhaps it was precisely because of his connection with the underworld that his statue did not stand on the hill, but in Podil close to the river.82

In following the problems connected with the Kyiv pantheon I came upon some further questions connected with Slavic religion, for example: what foreign influences in the formation of religious ideas can be discerned in the cult of the individual gods at a particular time? I clarify these questions only in so far as was necessary to fulfil the tasks set out in the introduction.

The report in Povesť vremennych let about the Kyiv pantheon relates to Vladimir's attempt to establish a state cult of the pagan gods, selecting for his pantheon deities suitable for a state-wide unifying ideology. It is therefore necessary to distinguish this state cult from folk belief and rites. The short time of its existence, and therefore the lack of data about it, makes it impossible to establish more concrete data about this state cult.
Mgr. Maroš Demko
